Grok To Media Man Australia

Media Man Australia is an Australian media, publicity, advertising, online publishing, and project management company based in Sydney (operating across areas like Maroubra Beach, Bondi, Newport Beach, and Palm Beach).

Media Man Australia forms part of the Media Man Group, established in 2001 by media entrepreneur Greg Tingle (often referred to as "Media Man").

The group includes entities like Media Man Australia, Media Man Int, Australian Sports Entertainment, Casino News Media, Bitcoin News Media, Eastern Suburbs Media, and others focused on niche publishing and services.

Key Focus Areas

Services: Publicity/PR campaigns, online advertising (text links, banners, etc.), SEO/SEM, content creation, website promotion, brand exposure, and project management.

They target niches like sports/entertainment (especially pro wrestling/combat sports), gaming/iGaming, pop culture, Bitcoin/crypto, tourism, and local Australian news.

Content: News articles, feature interviews (e.g., with wrestlers like Ken Shamrock, Dallas Page), profiles, multimedia, market updates, and monthly "awards" for sites, wrestlers, businesses, etc. Heavy coverage of WWE, UFC, movies, streaming, Google/SEO topics, and beach/local Sydney culture.

Media Man Group SEO

Media Man Group SEO refers to the Search Engine Optimization services, strategies, and content produced by the Media Man Group (including Media Man Int / Media Man International and Media Man Australia), founded in 2001 by Greg Tingle in Sydney, Australia.

Overview

The Media Man Group is a media, publicity, advertising, online publishing, and project management company with a strong focus on SEO (often playfully called “Hunt Machine Optimisation” by Greg Tingle). They have developed effective SEO techniques since launch, helping their own sites achieve Hitwise Australia “Top 10” status in the entertainment/personalities category.

https://t.co/MtxsUIBop2

They integrate SEO with PR, content marketing, niche publishing, link-building, and authority projects for sustainable, white-hat results. Their approach emphasizes organic growth over paid ads alone, adapting to Google’s evolving algorithms (including AI Overviews, Helpful Content updates, and Core Web Vitals).

Services Offered

Media Man Group provides:

SEO and content marketing — Keyword research, on-page optimization, evergreen/high-quality content creation, and topical authority building.

Online advertising and link strategies — Text link campaigns, niche media placement, and authority-building projects.

Integrated publicity — Combining SEO with PR, press releases, social media buzz, and brand exposure (often via their network of niche sites like wrestling, gaming, and entertainment portals).

Technical and adaptive SEO — Site structure, crawlability, mobile-friendliness, adaptation to AI search, and monitoring via Google Search Console.  Niche and local SEO — Tailored for sectors like pop culture, combat sports/wrestling, gaming, business, and entertainment.

They position SEO as part of broader “Putting Your Name (and Brand) Out There” campaigns, using their own platforms as case studies.

Greg Tingle’s SEO Philosophy (“Hunt Machine Optimisation”)

Greg Tingle (founder and lead) is a longtime SEO practitioner with 25+ years of experience. His practical, ethical, user-first approach includes:

High-quality, valuable content — Unique, evergreen, audience-focused material that serves user intent (“Do-Know-Go” queries) and builds E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness).

Technical foundations — Clean site structure, fast loading (Core Web Vitals), proper metadata, internal linking, and crawlability.

Authority and links — Quality backlinks via PR, content, and relationships rather than spammy tactics.

Adaptation to modern search — Monitoring Google updates, AI Overviews, conversational queries, and generative search. Focus on helpful content over keyword stuffing.

Sustainable organic growth — Organic SEO for long-term results, often outperforming or complementing paid ads.

He shares insights via blogs, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, and YouTube, frequently summarizing Google’s Search Off The Record podcast and other updates.

Key Strategies They Promote

From their sites and posts:

Keyword research — Target relevant, long-tail, and intent-based keywords; use tools like Google Keyword Planner or similar.

On-page SEO — Natural keyword use in titles, meta descriptions, headings, URLs, alt text, and content.

Content strategy — Create original, high-quality, regularly updated content; build topical authority in niches.

Technical SEO — Ensure mobile-friendliness, speed, proper indexing (monitor Search Console), and avoid issues like soft 404s or blocking.

Off-page and authority — Earn quality links, leverage PR/media placements, and build E-E-A-T signals. AI-era adaptation — Optimize for featured snippets, rich results, and AI Overviews; focus on user value and semantic relevance.  Monitoring and iteration — Use Google Search Console, Analytics, and track SERPs; test changes and monitor trends.

They often cover topics like indexing reports, Markdown vs. HTML for AI, lazy loading, and small business SEO.

Their SEO Content and Activity

Media Man Group actively produces and shares SEO resources:

Dedicated sections like SEO News and Search Engine Optimization pages on https://t.co/MtxsUIBop2 and related sites.

Frequent X posts summarizing Google updates, Search Off The Record episodes, and practical tips.

Monthly awards and spotlights that include “Search Engine Of The Month” (often Google).

Case studies through their own optimized network of sites (wrestling, markets, pop culture, etc.).

Their content is practical, gonzo-style journalism mixed with actionable advice, often tying SEO to publicity and niche media.

Summary

Media Man Group treats SEO as a core, integrated service alongside publicity and content creation.

Their long track record, focus on ethical/white-hat tactics, and adaptation to AI/search changes make them a niche player especially strong in entertainment, sports, and Australian/digital media sectors.

MIT’s GIFT framework improves CAD designs by turning its failures into training data | Rupendra Brahambhatt, Interesting Engineering

Creating a realistic 3D model from a simple image remains surprisingly difficult for artificial intelligence.

While AI can generate impressive pictures, producing the precise CAD code engineers use to design aircraft parts, cars, and consumer products is far more challenging. Even a small mistake can make a design unusable.

Now, researchers from MIT, IBM, and Red Hat have developed a framework that significantly improves the ability of AI systems to turn 2D images into functional CAD programs , producing more accurate designs while reducing inference computation by about 80 percent.

This new research work tackles one of the biggest obstacles in AI-driven engineering, which is the shortage of high-quality CAD training data. Existing image-to-CAD systems need vast numbers of examples linking 2D images to working CAD programs, but creating those datasets is expensive and labor-intensive.

Instead of relying on more human-created data, the new approach teaches AI using the mistakes it already makes. “We want to obtain data augmentation that is informed by the model itself,” lead study author and AI researcher Giorgio Giannone said .

Turning failed designs into training material

The team’s framework, called Geometric Inference Feedback Tuning (GIFT), works with vision-language models that convert a 2D image and text description into Python code that can be executed in CAD software to create a 3D object.

To understand where a model struggles, GIFT asks it to solve the same CAD problem multiple times in parallel. Some outputs are correct, some are close to the target design, and others are much further away.

According to the researchers, these ‘near-misses’ are the most valuable because they reveal exactly what the model does not yet understand.

The system executes each generated CAD program and compares the resulting 3D geometry with the target using a standard engineering metric known as Intersection over Union (IoU), which measures how closely two 3D shapes match.

Rather than discarding imperfect outputs, GIFT identifies those that are close to correct and uses them to generate new training examples.

Giannone explained, “If we sample the model 10 times and it generates 10 correct answers to the same problem, then there is not much for it to learn. We care about the in-between cases, where the model might only solve the problem 50 percent of the time.”

Teaching the model how to fix its own errors

GIFT improves the model through two complementary techniques. The first, called GIFT-REJECT, keeps alternative CAD programs that generate the correct geometry even if the code differs from the original reference solution.

Traditional AI training often assumes there is only one correct CAD program for each object, even though engineers can create the same part in many different ways. By exposing the model to multiple valid solutions, GIFT broadens its understanding of how CAD designs can be constructed.

The second method, GIFT-FAIL, focuses on imperfect outputs. The system takes a nearly correct 3D model generated by the AI, converts it back into an image, and pairs that image with the correct CAD program. By doing so, it creates new examples that effectively teach the model how to recover from specific mistakes.

More importantly, this process requires no human intervention. The framework automatically identifies errors, creates new training data, and uses that information to improve the model.

The researchers also designed GIFT around a technique known as inference-time scaling. Instead of retraining an entire AI model , which can be extremely expensive, the system improves performance during generation.

Rather than discarding the extra computation spent searching for better CAD programs, GIFT converts successful and near-successful attempts into new training examples that can later be used to improve the model through fine-tuning.

Moreover, users can decide how much computation they want to spend depending on their budget and time constraints.

Better CAD designs with a fraction of the computing power

When evaluated on the GenCAD-Code dataset, models enhanced with GIFT achieved a 12 percent improvement in geometric accuracy compared with a strong supervised-learning baseline.

The framework also reduced the inference computation needed to achieve comparable performance by about 80%.

“With GIFT, we started with geometry because with engineering problems, if the geometry of a 3D shape is not correct, nothing else will be correct, but there are many other aspects to consider,” Giannone said.

The system’s ability to learn from its own mistakes could help accelerate product development by making AI-generated CAD models more reliable.

Engineers could move more quickly from sketches to testable 3D designs, reducing development costs, shortening design cycles, and exploring a wider range of ideas without creating large amounts of new training data.

The researchers say this is only the beginning. So far, GIFT focuses on generating correct geometry, but future versions will aim to teach AI how to design parts that are not only accurate in shape but also easier to manufacture and better suited for real-world performance.

The study is published on arXiv .

How to Become an AI Engineer in 6 Months (Without Wasting Time)

Forget trying to learn everything.

The goal isn't to memorize AI buzzwords. The goal is to become someone who can build real AI products.

By the end of six months, you should be able to:

• Build LLM applications from scratch
• Work with OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-source models
• Design effective prompts and AI workflows
• Integrate tools, memory, and structured outputs
• Deploy production-ready AI applications

Here's a roadmap I'd recommend.

Month 1: Programming & Backend Foundations

Before touching advanced AI, become comfortable with the tools you'll use every day.

Learn:

• Python
• Git & GitHub
• Terminal / CLI
• HTTP, REST APIs & JSON
• Async programming basics
• SQL
• Pandas
• Virtual environments
• Error handling
• FastAPI (or Flask)

Build:

• A REST API
• A small automation tool
• A CRUD application

Month 2: LLM Application Development

Now start building with language models.

Learn:

• Prompt engineering
• System vs User messages
• Structured outputs (JSON)
• Function / Tool Calling
• Streaming responses
• Conversation memory
• Token usage & cost optimization
• Failure handling
• Prompt injection prevention

Projects:

• AI Chatbot
• Text Summarizer
• AI Writing Assistant

Month 3: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Most useful AI products rely on retrieval.

Learn:

• Embeddings
• Chunking strategies
• Vector databases
• Metadata filtering
• Hybrid search
• Reranking
• Hallucination reduction
• Grounded responses & citations

Projects:

• Chat with PDFs
• Documentation Assistant
• Internal Knowledge Base Chatbot

Month 4: AI Agents & Workflows

Agents are powerful, but only when used correctly.

Learn:

• Agent loops
• Tool selection
• State management
• Multi-step workflows
• Retry mechanisms
• Evaluation pipelines
• Success metrics
• When NOT to use agents

Projects:

• Research Agent
• Coding Assistant
• Multi-tool Workflow Automation

Month 5: Production & Deployment

Building locally isn't enough.

Learn:

• Production FastAPI
• Docker
• Background jobs
• Queues
• Authentication
• API security
• Logging
• Monitoring & observability
• Prompt versioning
• Cost monitoring
• Rate limiting
• Caching

Projects:

• Deploy an AI SaaS
• Add monitoring dashboards
• Support multiple users

Month 6: Choose Your Path

Don't try to master every area.

Pick one direction and go deep.

Direction 1: AI Product Engineer

Best for startup jobs.

Focus on:

• LLM applications
• RAG
• AI Agents
• Deployment
• Product UX

Direction 2: Applied AI / LLM Engineer

Focus on:

• Fine-tuning
• Prompting vs Fine-tuning
• Model evaluation
• Inference optimization
• Open-source models
• Training pipelines

Direction 3: AI Automation Engineer

Focus on:

• Workflow orchestration
• Multi-tool systems
• CRM automation
• Email & document automation
• Business process automation

This roadmap is only valuable if you actually build while learning.

Every concept should turn into a project.

By the end of six months, you'll have a portfolio full of real AI applications instead of just certificates.

Save this roadmap. You'll thank yourself later.

This is from the famous 2007 “CARET” (Commercial Applications Research for Extraterrestrial Technology) drone hoax/ARG by someone posting as “Isaac” from the fictional Palo Alto CARET Laboratory. https://t.co/yuBzP4O9NE 
The image you shared matches the well-known leaked “documents” and photos from that story: diagrams labeled LINGUISTIC ANALYSIS PRIMER (with hand-written numbers like #7128, #47129, arrows, nodes labeled A/B/E, circular “symbols,” flowing connections) and the Q4-85 Research Report showing what look like black ring-like components (with inscriptions such as “1-0.3+0.4A7.2+” etc.) alongside the physical 3D model of the spiky, legged “drone” artifact.
What the “language” is
•  It’s not a decipherable language or code. It’s artistic/technobabble created to look like a futuristic, context-sensitive “functional blueprint” system where symbols, shapes, and arrangements themselves supposedly act as the technology (no separate “programming” needed — the diagram is the device). https://t.co/yuBzP4O9NE 
•  The symbols mix geometric patterns, pseudo-alien glyphs (some resembling kana, circuit elements, or stylized letters/numbers), and flowing lines. Analysts who examined the full set noted:
•  Explicit numbering.
•  A character set size similar to a natural language alphabet.
•  Distribution patterns that look like typed technical text on curved paths (very Adobe Illustrator-esque). https://t.co/mj5IPsjSo5 
•  No consistent mapping or translation exists because it’s fabricated nonsense designed to evoke “alien engineering” — part of a detailed backstory involving reverse-engineered extraterrestrial tech from crash recoveries. The physical object is a prop (often described as looking like a mechanical virus or steampunk orb).
The whole thing was posted online (originally on a now-defunct site) as photos of supposed classified materials from the mid-1980s. It gained traction in UFO circles but has been thoroughly debunked as a creative hoax — fun and immersive, but not real.

Christopher Nolan gave Ludwig Göransson one instruction for The Odyssey: no orchestra. Not a stylistic preference, a flat ban. An instrument that didn’t exist in the Bronze Age couldn’t score a film set in it.
So Göransson had to build a musical language from instruments nobody alive has ever heard played correctly. The aulos, a double reed pipe carved into Greek pottery for a thousand years, has no surviving reeds. Musician Callum Armstrong spent weeks with two collaborators reading ancient source material just to work out how the mouthpiece functioned. The lyre, added at Nolan’s specific request to represent the pluck of Odysseus drawing his bow, was reconstructed the same way, performer Rosa Fragorapti describing the process as cross referencing iconography and philological sources against her own musicianship, because no continuous playing tradition survived to teach her directly.
Then Göransson added 35 bronze gongs sized to the Bronze Age setting, layered under synthesizers, and brought in James Blake for what he calls the score’s emotional pacing, a contemporary human voice inside a sonic world built entirely from instruments most audiences have never encountered.
None of this reads like a composer sprinkling in a historical flourish. It reads like archaeology performed in real time, a team reverse engineering how a civilization actually sounded from urns and carvings because the instruments and the people who knew how to play them are three thousand years gone. Göransson’s own line cuts through the research: the orchestra never existed back then, so the absence wasn’t a constraint to work around, it was the actual assignment.

The model humans prefer the most is not always the most accurate one!

Arena just added factuality scoring to their leaderboard alongside human preference. The idea: human preference measures whether a response felt good to read. Factuality measures the correctness of claims in a model's response. These are two different things.

Most benchmarks test models on fixed, predetermined questions in a lab setting. What Arena is doing differently: measuring factuality in real, open-ended user conversations at scale.

Over 2 million claims extracted from actual conversations, verified against the web, across 130k Text Arena battles and 40k Search Arena battles.

The way it works: they randomly sample battles, extract web-verifiable claims from each model response, verify them against the web, and calculate a factuality score per model. The final ranking is a weighted combination of human preference and factuality score.

When factuality weight is enabled, the shifts are significant. In Text Arena, GPT-5.5 jumps 13 spots. Muse Spark drops 13. Claude Fable 5 moves down slightly. In Search Arena, GPT-5.5-search takes the top spot while Gemini grounding drops from 7 to 13.

I've shared the full methodology blog in the replies!

Shifts we observe with factuality:

While human preference scores across nearly all providers have been climbing over time, plotting pure factuality score against flagship model release date shows OpenAI is the only provider also consistently improving factuality over an extended period. SpacexAI and Meta have also been improving with their recent releases.
